Gurus, friends, sons, servants, relatives,
and kinsmen have been slain by us, who sought wealth, while we ourselves remain as mere shells of our bodies.

for Kuntī told me that he was her brother, born of the Sun.

now, thinking "this man has feet like Kuntī’s," it has attained gentleness.

fie on this kingdom of mine, which is now nothing but another name for hell! (Bhājana 13.11)

"This must be understood by a Brahmin," he said; thus addressed, he became distressed and, quickly assuming the guise of a Brahmin, went to the hermitage of Jamadagni's son. (Bhājana 13.15)
Then that descendant of Bhrigu, having requested the Brahma-weapon,
wandered for a long time as an archer upon the ridges of Mount Mahendra.
Once, a certain brahmin, having incurred sin through ignorance,
became utterly enraged and cursed him for his mistreatment of the sacrificial cow.
"Since you have, out of delusion, wronged my sacrificial cow while I was occupied with my enemy, therefore the earth shall swallow your wheel."
Thus cursed by the Brahmin, as if burning incessantly,
he performed great austerities and, having propitiated Rāma, obtained the Brahmāstra.
Then, on one occasion, having become weary from his ascetic observances, the son of Bhṛgu placed his head upon Karṇa’s lap and fell asleep.
In the meantime, a harsh and unbearable worm named Malarka—emaciated, with sharp fangs, lips, and feet—bitten him. (Bhājana 13.21)
While he endured that agony, startled by his teacher’s awakening,
the descendant of Bhrigu, drenched in that blood, abandoned his sleep.
Agitated, wondering "What is this?", and his eyes narrowed by the touch of blood,
he beheld Rādheya bitten and possessed of a distorted form.
Then, as soon as he was seen by Rāma, that red-necked, blazing-eyed rākṣasa worm was reduced to ashes in an instant.
He said: "In the past, I, a foe of the gods named Gṛdhra, lusted after the wife of Bhr̥gu out of fickleness; I was then cursed by the sage. (Bhājana-mālā 13.25)
O Lord, due to that curse he went to hell and entered this sinful womb;
it has now reached its end through the sight of you, and it has been exhausted.
When the Rākṣasa had departed after saying this, Bhārgava asked Karṇa:
"Who are you? You are surely not a twice-born; you must be a Kṣatriya capable of enduring intense pain."
Hearing this, Karṇa was startled and revealed his own lineage and name to him; thereupon, the preceptor immediately cursed him in anger.
"Since you obtained the Brahmā-weapon through the deception of a brahmin,
it shall meet its destruction within your own limits."
Having been repulsed by the descendant of Bhṛgu, Karṇa approached Suyodhana;
out of affection born from rivalry with you, he was made a lord over his limbs by him.
In former times, relying upon the strength of his arms, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra abducted the daughter of Citrāṅgada, the king of Kaliṅga.
At that svayaṃvara, when Duryodhana had already departed, Karṇa alone first challenged the enraged circle of kings out of pride.
Having conquered all the kings, that treasury of glory, exulting in his strength, brought Jarāsaṃdha to the swing of doubt by means of wrestling.
Defeated, Jarāsaṃdha gave him the city of Mālinī;
and other heroic lords of men likewise surrendered their respective portions.
He was deceived by the lord of the gods, who stripped him of his armor and earrings,
and had previously been cursed by the preeminent brahmin, his teacher Bhārgava.
Addressed by Kuntī with wise counsel, yet disregarded by the son of Gaṅgā,
he was made to hear harsh words from Śalya for the sake of quelling his fiery spirit.
The wise one was slain by the son of Śakra through divine weapons and his own dark-minded stratagem;
otherwise, who could have killed him in battle, given his formidable prowess?
When this had been told by Nārada, Kuntī, casting aside her grief for her son through fortitude, spoke to the son of Dharma who was afflicted with sorrow.
Though entreated by Ravi as well, he did not perceive the need for peace due to the power of destiny;
that constant hater of yours was personally disregarded by me.
"He has gone to the abode of the Sun, slain face-to-face in battle. Do not grieve; you have now attained [the throne], so enjoy the kingdom without anxiety."
Finding no peace as he contemplated the many virtues of Karṇa, he said:
"Because of our mother’s concealment, this elder brother of ours was unknown to us."
Therefore, women will always have their [sexual] impulses severed;
they shall subsist on alms or fruits and roots, their livelihoods being unrestrained.

alas, like dogs, we have brought about a terrible total destruction."

he was separated from friends and kin, and entered the ocean of saṃsāra, which is filled with fierce crocodiles.

With eyes copper-red with anger, he looked at the earth for a moment and said:
"Alas! For those cursed by the gods, even at the end, sufferings exceed their pleasures."
Thus, being utterly deprived by fate, they all grieve;
this renunciation of yours now serves only as a source of laughter in the assemblies of the virtuous.
For one who seeks wealth that has been lost, for one who abandons prosperity already attained, and for those sinking into impotent actions contrary to their station— Bhāj 13.50.
Renunciation is called the laziness of those who procrastinate;
what else in this world is more shameful and more despised by the wise?
That a man should so quickly abandon everything like a drunkard casting off his garment—
this unprecedented course you have undertaken is excessive in its calamity.
"Never indeed have we heard that a king subsists on alms; O King, enjoy this prosperity obtained by succession without any agitation."
Sacrificial rites, acts of giving, and other such deeds belong only to the wealthy and fortunate;
for one who has lost his wealth is indeed pitiable, yet not so one who has lost his life.
One who possesses wealth for but a moment is truly dead; one who is forever destitute is always dead.
O King, even one like Māndhātṛ or Nahuṣa is no more than this earth.

subsisting on bits of withered leaves as food, equanimous, and indifferent to the pleasant and the unpleasant.
That celibate student, wandering among the deer sporting in the forest,
remained silent with his attachments dissolved, thinking of nothing at all in his mind.
"I shall become a silent sage, abstaining from food for the sake of destroying cyclic existence"—
to the king who was speaking thus, the son of the Wind-god replied:
Alas, O King, your intellect is as stubborn in its evil grasp as that of a fool; why was this wisdom not employed by you before causing the destruction of the earth?

O King, when the city has been consumed by fire, what is the use of a water-drawing machine? You, who have renounced everything and are no longer in the final stage of life, do not shine [by such means].
Like an *aśoka* tree in the month of spring whose leaves have suddenly withered,
he then obtained this earth through the exertion of a wager involving his own life.
What else can be said of you who, out of delusion, disdainfully abandon [the path] while disregarding the pressure of obstacles? After a long time, he finally reached that treasure.
O King, why do you kick it? That which has gone can never be recovered again;
having brought back that which is beloved through various sacrifices of life, it must inevitably depart.
Just as one intoxicated by honey lies down, so are you intent on acting;
yet, with your soul deceived by renunciation, you ought not to abandon your steadfastness.
If liberation belongs to those who have abandoned all action, then no liberated beings are seen;
what else could it be? At that very moment, we would all have fallen into calamity.
Just as you were once desirous of a village when you were made our eldest by the Creator, so too,
having formerly been desirous of a village in the forest, you are now eager for the forest in the village.
They do not remain on the lap nor upon the shoulder, like a distressed child;
householders who possess the nature of goodness and abide in their own duties are liberated.
"When it was said by Bhīmasena that deer and elephants in the forest did not go to heaven when seen [by him], Dhanañjaya spoke again."
"O King, liberation exists in the home for the blessed who eat the remnants of offerings;
formerly, there were young sons of Brahmins who had not yet grown their beards."
Having resorted to dispassion at an improper time, they went to the forest and entered the religious life;
while they were there with their hearts filled with compassion, Purandara, assuming the form of a bird, appeared before them.

Having heard the speech of Śuka, whose chest was golden, the twice-born praised householders who subsist on the remains of sacrificial food (vighasa) in their practice of that [dharma]. (Bhājana 13.72)
The fools, overjoyed, considered themselves to be eaters of sacrificial remnants (vighasāśinaḥ).
Then Śakuni, being questioned by them, spoke as if laughing: Bhāj 13.73.
Rough, emaciated, and smeared with dirt, you lead a life of hardship in the forest;
you are perpetual partakers of suffering alone, for you do not subsist on the remains of sacrificial offerings.

Those householders who divide their food into morning and evening portions according to rule, and eat only what remains after providing for their dependents and guests, are blessed; they are the eaters of *vighasa*.
By their boundless merits, eternal worlds exist in heaven;
from them, all householders of the various stages of life live, like creatures from a cloud.
Having been thus instructed by the Vajrī in his own form,
those twice-born ones abandoned their forest dwelling and returned to their own homes.
"You understand the course of all phenomena and know the truth of the masters;
likewise, O protector of the earth, you ought not to abandon your steadfastness."
When Arjuna had spoken thus, the two sons of Mādrī then said:
"Enjoy this kingdom without effort, for its thorns have been removed."
"O lord of the earth, victor of universal sovereignty, performer of sacrifices, protect the subjects!"—
when these words were spoken by the twins, his beloved and affectionate wife [replied] to her husband.
Draupadī, speaking sweetly, addressed the son of Dharma:
"Your heroic brothers, possessing the splendor of the gods, are obedient to your command."
"Behold, out of lack of enthusiasm, these men falsely depict the earth;
for such difficult deeds as they performed with vigor in battle [could not be so easily achieved]. (Bhājana 13.82)
Therefore, you ought to make this day fruitful for us by granting a share of the kingdom,
for we now stand with our faces cast down, sighing, and suffering from the fruitlessness of our endeavors.
O King, honoring their prowess with affectionate words and applauding it,
you, whose conduct is never weak, should enjoy this kingdom acquired by your own arms.
"Devote yourself to the prosperity arising from victory; cowards are not the recipients of wealth.
When Kṛṣṇā had spoken thus, Jiṣṇu addressed the king once more.
By protecting the world, kings rightly go to heaven;
it is through fear of royal punishment that subjects engage in their own duties.
Where the dark, red-eyed Punishment is present, people devour one another like fish, being devoid of restraint.
In that state, through the Vedas and sacrifices, the perfections of dharma increase;
and by those various appropriate austerities, they obtain the fruit belonging to those of tranquil splendor.
That very [king] was formerly the progenitor of Daṇḍadhāra, the king who was his dharma-brother; he had turned away from sovereignty and desired to depart for the forest.
His wife, who spoke of dharma, spoke sweetly out of affection:
"O King, there is no liberation in the forest, nor is there bondage in homes."
For the discerning who are engaged in their own duty, liberation is [attained];
yet those who have shaved their heads while their desires remain unshorn, and who are stained by impurities both within and without, are not liberated.
Those who display the banner of righteousness out of hypocrisy are called "preachers of dharma" by those who speak of dharma;
therefore, even while you are ruling a kingdom, you must always [behave accordingly].
"The destruction of cyclic existence is attainable by one who is truly unattached and happy";
having been told this by his wife, the King of Mithilā took refuge in the state of liberation while living.
When Phalguna had thus declared that even one who has renounced his kingdom may attain the supreme, eternal abode, the gods present there offered their praise.
And the sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana declared the dharma of active engagement:
"O lord of the earth, the proper protection of your subjects is your own specific duty."
The departure of kings for the forest at an improper time results in the ruin of their reign;
yet kings such as Sudyumna and others attained success through their subjects.
Unaffected by the hardships of asceticism, because they administered justice correctly,
those two brothers were formerly excellent sages, experts in the Vedas and the Smṛtis.
Once, Śaṅkha and Likhita, who were firm in their vows and refined in their conduct,
went to their brother’s hermitage and personally took a tree from it.
Having written out the fruits [of his actions], he ate them out of delusion as if out of affection;
approaching him, Śaṅkha, agitated by the fear of falling away from dharma, spoke to him.
"You do not realize that this is theft; why do you eat the fruit of another?
Go, O brother, and confess the evil deed you have committed to the king yourself."
Thus addressed by him, Likhita informed King Sudyumna that he himself was seeking punishment for eating the fruit, once he had heard what had transpired.
The lord of the earth said to him: "O Blessed One, you who observe extensive vows are the authority regarding all matters of dharma; go in purity, by virtue of my boon."
Though thus addressed by the king, he, fearing a lapse from virtuous conduct, repeatedly requested the lord of men for punishment alone.
Then the lord of the earth ordered the cutting off of his hand;
with his hand severed, he went joyfully into the presence of his brother.
And at his word, having bathed and performed the two birth-rites, I would give [the gift];
through the power of his asceticism, he became one whose fever of latent defilements was stilled.
Sudyumna also, the lord of subjects and a treasury of glory, attained worlds befitting his asceticism through the proper wielding of punishment.
***** The Narrative of Sudyumna ***** Therefore, O protector of the earth, remaining established in the duty of a Kṣatriya, protect your subjects;
and seeing that destruction is brought about by Time, do not set your mind on grief. (Bhagavadgītāmṛtavyākhyā 13.107)
Having come into being again and again, the worlds are indeed dissolved by time; this labor of existence is wondrous, like the waters of the divisions of time.
"O King, it was said long ago by the discerning King Senajit:
'One should fix the mind firmly upon suffering; this is the medicine for the diseases of grief and lamentation.'"
For those who grieve and lack fortitude, peace never arises;
for them, sorrows come upon sorrows, just as riches bring further riches to men.
Having seen the arising and passing away of living beings in this world at their respective times—
like the ripening of fruits— who that possesses knowledge of reality would grieve, O knower of time?
Long ago, when questioned by Janaka, the brahmin Aśmaka replied:
"The discerning do not grieve over phenomena that perish by their very nature."
Among both the stationary and the moving, no one is seen who is able to transcend the limit set for their lifespan by Time.
Wealth, lifespan, the body, birth, and likewise youthfulness,
undergo various forms of reversal due to the diversity of time.
The high become low, and those who were united fall apart;
indeed, by the power of time, the low-lying become elevated and the elevated sink down.
Those of low lineage attain noble birth, the wealthy fall into poverty, fools acquire scholarship, and the fortunate likewise encounter misfortune. (Bhājana-mālā 13.116)
Kings are seen to have very short lifespans, while the poor live for a hundred years;
even those experts in elixirs are observed to be broken by old age.
The wealthy are tormented by disease, while the poor remain free from ailment;
even those who know the science of Ayurveda pass away in their very youth.
Fools become devoted to virtuous conduct, while the learned are devoid of dharma;
indeed, through various such reversals brought about by time, these things occur.
Even the gods, headed by the four-faced Brahmā, who are the creators of the three worlds,
are not able to protect one who has been marked by the sidelong glance of Time.
For those who are wealthy and those with little wealth, for the wise and those of dull intellect,
the purchase in the marketplace of Time is indeed equal, for it is devoid of affection.
In the forest of worldly existence, for embodied beings tossed about by the winds of time,
comings and goings constantly occur among one another, like those of trees.
If those who have come together unexpectedly perish unexpectedly,
what cause for grief is there for living beings, since coming and going is indeed constant?
Indeed, those possessed of discernment should not feel anguish at separations;
for in this world, all existing things are momentary and perishable, experienced only through their non-existence.
Having said, "By Aśmaka," the Lord of Sages ceased speaking and looked intently at Yudhiṣṭhira, who was consumed by deep sorrow.
***** The Song of Aśmaka // 2 // ***** Then,
urged by Arjuna out of affection, the lotus-eyed Blessed One, the enemy of Kaiṭabha, spoke to the son of Dharma. Bhājana 13.126.
O King, do not indulge in vain despondency that withers the body;
for those slain heroes, there is no returning again from sorrow.
Some depart today at dawn, others later, and still others yet later;
all go into the boundless cycle of existence—whom should anyone mourn, and for what reason?
Surely everyone, out of delusion, considers themselves to be imperishable;
for even when their destruction is right before them, the perishable one does not grieve for what is already lost.
Those people, those powers, and those blazing fortunes have indeed been reduced by Time, with effortless ease, to nothing more than a memory.
In the past, this blessed Nārada spoke out of compassion to the king named Sṛñjaya, who was overwhelmed with grief for his son.
O King, why do you grieve for your son who has reached his appointed end?
At the final limit, the entire world, including ourselves, shall cease to exist.
After some time, King Matutta passed away;
during his reign, the gods, including Indra, were present on earth as participants in his sacrificial assemblies.
To him Indra rained down gold for an entire year;
he whose officiating priest was Saṃvarta, the brother of Bṛhaspati.
And Suhotra, the lord of the earth, has reached the state of being a mere memory—
he who made the earth truly "Vasumatī" (the possessor of wealth) by means of showers of gold.
And King Bṛhadratha, the best of chariot-warriors, set out for his home;
at whose sacrifice the Lord of the Gods, having drunk the Soma, attained great joy.
Śibi Auśīnara, who ruled the earth under a single umbrella,
has become one whose name remains only as fame— he, the foremost among all givers, has passed away.
Even that Bharata, who performed a thousand horse-sacrifices and a hundred Rājasūya sacrifices, departed for the third heaven in the course of time.
And that Rāma, son of Daśaratha, the destroyer of the lineage of the ten-necked Rāvaṇa,
has reached the final stage, his virtues being sung by the gods.
And King Bhagīratha, by whose ascetic penance he brought the Ganges down from the head of Śaṅkara, has passed away according to the will of Time.
That lord of the earth, Dilīpa, also reached the state of mindfulness,
he at whose golden sacrificial post the inhabitants of heaven danced.
And King Māndhātṛ, that conqueror of all, was not born from a womb;
even Śakra and the other gods were surpassed by him in his wondrous prowess.
In time, even King Yayāti,
that hero who slew the enemies of the gods in the battle between the gods and asuras, met his dissolution.
That King Ambarīṣa entered the body of Yaśas,
he whose unfading command kings bore like a garland.
That king Śaśabindu also reached the end of his life;
he had a hundred million sons whose splendor was like that of Indra.
King Gaya also went there, who gave away the earth made of gold;
and the number of his sacrifices cannot be fully recounted.
And as Rantideva set forth for his sacrifices with the hides of animals,
the sacred river Carmaṇvatī was set flowing by him from those streams.
And that king Sagara,
by whom the oceans were made [famous] through his sixty thousand sons who served as guardians of the horse, has passed away.
And Vainya, who separated the mountains with the tip of his bow—that king Śakrādhipa also abandoned his dear war. (Bhājana 13.149)
These and other kings have been swallowed up by time;
do not grieve, O Sṛñjaya, for at my word let your son live.
Having spoken thus, Nārada, that ocean of compassion, restored the king’s son Kanakaṣṭhīvin to life and granted him a lifespan of a thousand years.

Being thus questioned by the Son of Dharma (Yudhiṣṭhira), the Four-Armed One (Viṣṇu) spoke again: Bhājana-mālā 13.152.
Likewise, the two celestial rishis Nārada and Parvata, wandering through the world of mortals, resided in the house of King Sṛñjaya.
There, the two of them, full of affection and overflowing with love, joyfully shared with one another all that was in their hearts, reaching a mutual understanding.
Sṛñjaya assigned his daughter Sukumārī, who was adorned with beauty and whose name was truly significant, to attend upon him.
Gazing without blinking at that young woman who was moving about— she whose eyes were like those of a doe and whose hair was as dark as a peacock's neck— Nārada became overwhelmed by love.
His nephew Parvata quickly perceived with his eye of wisdom that state of mind within him which he was concealing out of shame.
Then, enraged by the violation of his boundary, he cursed his maternal uncle:
"You shall become the husband of this delicate woman in the form of a monkey."
Thus cursed by him in anger, Nārada in turn cursed his sister’s son out of wrath, saying: "May you not go to heaven."
Then, after some time, Nārada received from Sṛñjaya the maiden who had been offered to him; having obtained her at the time of marriage, he became such [a man] in an instant.
Having obtained such a husband as Nārada,
that virtuous woman regarded him with undivided mind as a cascading stream of nectar for her eyes.
Having mutually appeased their curse and the surge of their anger having subsided,
they both became composed through affection, casting off their agitation.
Having abandoned her monkey form, the delicate and devoted wife,
filled with apprehension, waited for a long time before approaching Nārada once she had learned his story.
"Therefore, let this Nārada himself tell the remainder of the story.
When Kṛṣṇa had spoken thus and ceased, Yudhiṣṭhira questioned him.

Then, by virtue of our boon, Sṛñjaya’s son Kāñcanasṭhīvī went forth according to his true purpose; Śatakratu could not withstand him.
By chance, on the bank of the Jahnavī, the Lord of the Gods killed that infant— who was intent on play— with his thunderbolt in the form of a tiger.
Seeing his lotus-eyed son slain, Sṛñjaya grieved,
his mind overwhelmed by distress, exhaustion, and fainting.
Seeing that king distressed and talkative with lamentation,
I compassionately restored his son, Suvarṇaṣṭhīvin, to life.
By my boon, having enjoyed this earth for a lifespan of a thousand years, he departed for heaven in the course of time; for embodied beings do not remain forever.

***** The Narrative of Svarṇaṣṭhīvin // 4 // ***** When this had been told by Nārada and Vyāsa had also consoled him again and again, the son of Dharma, still afflicted by grief, spoke once more: (Bhājana 13.171)
Fie on us, blinded by greed, who have fallen into this perilous mire of sin,
by whom the destruction of our teachers, kinsmen, and children was brought about through a desire for enjoyments!
I believe that by repeatedly offering this sinful body into the fire, it will go to its destruction; yet the sin of killing Bhīṣma will not [be destroyed]. (Bhājana 13.173)
To Yudhiṣṭhira, who was thus overcome by the fire of grief and lamenting,
the sage, son of Parāśara, spoke for the sake of maintaining the world's order.
For kings who live by war, the slaying of enemies is their constant duty;
having performed the task appropriate to your lineage, do not indulge in vain despair.
Through hymns of praise, repentance, powerful rites of atonement,
gifts, and ablutions at sacred fords, there is a remedy for sins.
But you, O King, having abandoned your own dharma, are defiled;
therefore, perform the horse sacrifice even if you suspect it to be false.
Protect the subjects with confidence, as well as the women who have lost their protectors;
look upon the daughters of those whose sons were slain by enemies as if they were your own children.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One, the sage whose disturbances were stilled, being questioned again by the king,
spoke once more of the pacification of all evils.

is released from the intense fear of killing a Brahmin at the conclusion of his vow.

one who has violated the Guru’s bed is liberated by lying upon a crest of flame the color of fire.

like rivers swept away by a great flood, they become pure in heart.

Having rejoiced in your own kingdom and secured the support of the subjects, go to Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu; he will explain the duties to you.
Thus addressed by Dvaipāyana and enlightened by Kṛṣṇa,
he entered the city with his followers, placing Dhṛtarāṣṭra at the head.
Being honored by the subjects and praised by the bards,
he reached the capital city and entered the beautiful assembly hall.
There, having placed Dhaumya— the foremost of family priests— at their head, he honored the Brahmins who had arrived there of their own accord and were bestowing abundant blessings.

Thus Janārdana, with a voice as deep as a thundercloud, spoke slowly to the daughter of Jahnu, who was making such lamentations, comforting her.
O Goddess, though you have realized the ultimate truth and are a witness even to the curse of Vasu,
why do you become bewildered like an ordinary mother?
Indeed, Śikhaṇḍin had no power to slay Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, who possessed the prowess of the enemy of Tripura, except through the agency of Time, which is more powerful than all.
Having himself attained the supreme abode and met his death by his own will, do not grieve for your son who is beyond sorrow; for who else could be born such as he?
Thus consoled gradually by Kṛṣṇa along with Vyāsa and the others,
the Mandākinī shone for a moment, its fish and sea-monsters having ceased their movement.
Then, having taken leave of her, those led by Yudhiṣṭhira, accompanied by their followers,
returned overwhelmed with grief once the lord of the day had set.
Thus ends the section on the Duties of Giving within the Śāntiparvan;
the Śāntiparvan is completed.
